meta.title: Who really said "Baseball is the only field of endeavor where a man can succeed three times out of ten and be considered a good performer"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited everywhere to Ted Williams, but no speech, book or interview has ever been produced for it. Here is the paper trail, and what he really wrote.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Baseball is the only field of endeavor where a man can succeed three times out of ten and be considered a good performer'?
meta.ogDescription: No source has ever been produced for this Ted Williams line. The paper trail, the wording drift, and the sentence he really did write about hitting .300.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1918–2002 · Boston Red Sox hitter · Hall of Fame, 1966
answer.sourceLine: Every quote site credits Ted Williams, no one else is ever named, and the thought is unmistakably his — but no speech, book, interview or column has been produced for this wording. The earliest printings located are sports-quotation and motivational compilations, from 1984 onward, and the citation most sites inherit points only to a reference work published in 2006. Williams did make the same point in print, in a different sentence, in The Science of Hitting.

source.excerpt: Baseball is the only field of endeavor where a man can succeed three times out of ten and be considered a good performer.
trail: Wikiquote’s Ted Williams article ↗ does not carry this line at all — not among its sourced quotations, and not among the ones it flags as misattributed. Quote Investigator has never taken the quote up either. So there is no specialist finding to defer to, in either direction.

The citation the web runs on is thin. Baseball Almanac ↗ is the rare aggregator that gives a book and page for each quote, and for this one it can offer only The 2006 ESPN Baseball Encyclopedia, page 5 — a reference work, not a Williams utterance on a datable occasion.
It is not in his Hall of Fame speech: the full 1966 induction transcript ↗ contains neither ‘endeavor’ nor ‘three times out of ten’.

Full-text search of the Internet Archive’s scanned books ↗ returns the phrase overwhelmingly in quotation, trivia, motivational and coaching compilations, the earliest a sports-quotation dictionary of 1984; the handful of scholarly appearances among the hits — a 1985 Texas Christian University Press readings anthology, the proceedings of the 1990 Cooperstown Symposium — themselves quote it without a source. It appears in neither of Williams’s own digitized books, though both are in that same corpus. What the corpus does hold is his real version of the idea, in The Science of Hitting ↗.
source.excerptNote: Printed here as it circulates. There is no original text behind it to quote from — the sentence exists only in quotation compilations and, from there, across the web.

sourceLink.text: The Science of Hitting on the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: Copyright follows a source, and no source has been identified: this wording cannot be tied to any dated speech, book or interview, so no rights status can honestly be asserted — and it should certainly not be assumed public domain. Williams’s own published books, the 1969 memoir My Turn at Bat and the hitting manual The Science of Hitting, both written with John Underwood, are firmly in United States copyright, held by his estate together with Simon & Schuster.

author.name: Ted Williams
author.heading: Who Ted Williams was
author.metaLine: 1918–2002 · Boston Red Sox outfielder, the last man to hit .400
author.bio: Theodore Samuel Williams was born in San Diego in 1918 and spent his entire major-league career with the Boston Red Sox, from 1939 to 1960, hitting .344 lifetime with 521 home runs, winning two Triple Crowns and two MVP awards, and batting .406 in 1941 — still the last .400 season in the majors. He lost most of five seasons to military service as a naval aviator and Marine Corps pilot in the Second World War and Korea, and was elected to the Hall of Fame on the first ballot in 1966. He was also an unusually articulate technician of his own craft: with the sportswriter John Underwood he produced the memoir My Turn at Bat (1969) and the hitting manual The Science of Hitting, which is why lines about the arithmetic of batting get pinned to him so readily.

copyAttribution: "Baseball is the only field of endeavor where a man can succeed three times out of ten and be considered a good performer." — attributed to Ted Williams (1918–2002). No primary source has been located; the earliest printings found are sports-quotation and motivational compilations, from 1984 onward. Williams made the same point in his own words in "The Science of Hitting," where he notes that even a .300 hitter is going to fail at his job seven out of ten times. Via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: What is actually wrong here
misattribution.intro: No rival claimant exists — nobody else has ever been credited with this sentence. What fails is the sourcing: the line is presented as documented Williams when nothing documents it.

items.why: Baseball Almanac ↗, the site most quote pages copy from, cites this line to The 2006 ESPN Baseball Encyclopedia, page 5. That is a reference book published in 2006 — a place the quote had already arrived, not a record of Williams saying it. Downstream sites such as Goodreads ↗ give no citation at all, and note that their quotes are community-added and unverified.

items.scope: The speech it is assumed to come from
items.who: Ted Williams, Hall of Fame induction, 25 July 1966
items.why: His induction address is the speech people reach for when they want a Williams aphorism with an occasion attached. The full transcript ↗ contains no ‘field of endeavor’ and no ‘three times out of ten’; its famous line is about baseball giving every American boy a chance to excel.

Printed versions disagree with one another. Full-text search of the Internet Archive’s books ↗ shows Glenn Liebman’s compilations printing ‘field of endeavor in which a man can succeed’, Wayne Stewart’s adding ‘and still be considered a good performer’, and Kerry Banks’s trivia book shortening it to ‘the only endeavor where’. Text copied from a page does not wobble like that.

misattribution.truthLine: Williams did put the same arithmetic on the record, in his own words and in a book you can open: in The Science of Hitting ↗, written with John Underwood, he observes that even a .300 hitter — a rare item, he adds — is going to “fail at your job seven out of ten times”. Same point, different sentence, real source.

context.heading: Why the line sticks to him
lead: Baseball really is the arithmetic oddity the sentence describes. A hitter who makes an out seven times in ten is a .300 hitter, and a .300 hitter is a good one; in almost any other job, failing seventy per cent of the time ends the job. That is a genuinely strange fact about the sport, and it wants a spokesman.

Ted Williams is the obvious candidate, because he is the man who came closest to beating the arithmetic — .406 in 1941, .344 for a career — and because he wrote a whole book about the mechanics of hitting. When a piece of baseball wisdom needs an author, the greatest hitter who ever lived is the path of least resistance. That is exactly the mechanism by which unsourced lines find famous homes.
context.detailsSummary: What the paper trail actually shows
detailsBody: A full-text search of the Internet Archive’s scanned books turns up roughly sixty printings of this sentence. They are overwhelmingly quotation collections, trivia books, motivational titles and coaching guides — the genre that recycles rather than reports — and the handful of scholarly and general-trade exceptions, such as a 1985 Texas Christian University Press readings anthology and the proceedings of the 1990 Cooperstown Symposium, quote the line without a source of their own. The earliest is Andrew J. Maikovich’s Sports Quotations (McFarland, 1984), which already prints the exact wording and credits Williams — twenty-four years after his last game.

The wording will not hold still across them. Glenn Liebman’s compilations print ‘the only field of endeavor in which a man can succeed’; Wayne Stewart’s has ‘and still be considered a good performer’; Kerry Banks’s trivia book trims it to ‘the only endeavor where’. Lines copied from a printed page do not drift like that. Lines passed between quote books do.
Meanwhile the phrase appears in neither My Turn at Bat nor The Science of Hitting, both of which are in the same searchable corpus — so the silence is a real absence rather than a gap in coverage.
context.pull: A quote that keeps changing its own wording is a quote nobody is copying from a page.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Ted Williams article contains neither "field of endeavor" nor "three times out of ten", in any section including Misattributed/Disputed.
Baseball Almanac carries this quote and cites it to The 2006 ESPN Baseball Encyclopedia, by Pete Palmer, Sterling Publishers, February 25, 2006, page 5.

The full transcript of Ted Williams's 25 July 1966 Hall of Fame induction speech contains no occurrence of "endeavor" or "three times out of ten"; its famous line is that baseball gives every American boy a chance to excel.

Internet Archive full-text book search for "three times out of ten and be considered" returns about 59 results, overwhelmingly quotation, trivia, motivational or coaching compilations (e.g. The Bathroom Baseball Book, Baseball Shorts, Play Ball!, Red Sox Triviology) crediting Ted Williams, with a few scholarly and general-trade exceptions (Sport Inside Out, TCU Press 1985; Cooperstown Symposium on Baseball and the American Culture 1990; Plimpton, The Norton Book of Sports) that quote it without a source; none of the 59 is a text written by Williams. The earliest is Andrew J. Maikovich, Sports Quotations: Maxims, Quips and Pronouncements for Writers and Fans (Jefferson, N.C.: McFarland, 1984), id sportsquotations0000maik, whose snippet reads "endeavor where a man can succeed three times out of ten and be considered a good performer. — Ted Williams".

Internet Archive full-text search for "succeed three times out of ten" shows competing printed wordings: "field of endeavor in which a man can succeed" (Glenn Liebman), "and still be considered a good performer" (Wayne Stewart), and "the only endeavor where" (Kerry Banks). The Science of Hitting is NOT among the 64 results of this search, as expected: the circulating wording does not occur in Williams's own book.

Internet Archive full-text search for "fail at your job seven" returns The Science of Hitting by Ted Williams, id scienceofhitting00will, with the snippet "you are going to fail at your job seven out of ten times?" — the documented Williams wording of the same idea.

Andrew J. Maikovich, Sports Quotations: Maxims, Quips and Pronouncements for Writers and Fans, was published by McFarland, Jefferson, N.C., in 1984; and David L. Vanderwerken and Spencer K. Wertz, Sport Inside Out: Readings in Literature and Philosophy, by Texas Christian University Press, Fort Worth, in 1985, printing the variant "succeed only three times out of ten and be considered an outstanding performer".
The Science of Hitting is by Ted Williams and John Underwood, published by Simon & Schuster, New York; the digitized copy is the revised and updated Fireside edition of 1986.
Goodreads displays the quote attributed to Ted Williams with no book, speech or source citation, and states that its quotes are added by the community and not verified.

Ted Williams was born 30 August 1918 in San Diego and died 5 July 2002; he played for the Boston Red Sox 1939-1960, batted .344 lifetime with 521 home runs, hit .406 in 1941, won two MVP awards and two Triple Crowns, served as a naval aviator and Marine Corps pilot, and was elected to the Hall of Fame in 1966.
The Baseball Hall of Fame's page for Ted Williams gives his biography and career record; it does not contain the phrase "field of endeavor" or "three times out of ten".
